{{Short description|Group homomorphism up to bounded error}}
{{more footnotes|date=March 2022}}

In [[group theory]], given a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math>, a '''quasimorphism''' (or '''quasi-morphism''') is a [[Function (mathematics)|function]] <math>f:G\to\mathbb{R}</math> which is [[additive map|additive]] up to bounded error, i.e. there exists a [[Constant (mathematics)|constant]] <math>D\geq 0</math> such that <math>|f(gh)-f(g)-f(h)|\leq D</math> for all <math>g, h\in G</math>. The least positive value of <math>D</math> for which this inequality is satisfied is called the '''defect''' of <math>f</math>, written as <math>D(f)</math>. For a group <math>G</math>, quasimorphisms form a [[linear subspace|subspace]] of the [[function space]] <math>\mathbb{R}^G</math>.

== Examples ==
* [[Group homomorphism]]s and [[bounded function]]s from <math>G</math> to <math>\mathbb{R}</math> are quasimorphisms. The sum of a group homomorphism and a bounded function is also a quasimorphism, and functions of this form are sometimes referred to as "trivial" quasimorphisms.<ref>Frigerio (2017), p. 12.</ref>
* Let <math>G=F_S</math> be a [[free group]] over a set <math>S</math>. For a reduced word <math>w</math> in <math>S</math>, we first define the big counting function <math>C_w:F_S\to \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}</math>, which returns for <math>g\in G</math> the number of copies of <math>w</math> in the reduced representative of <math>g</math>. Similarly, we define the little counting function <math>c_w:F_S\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}</math>, returning the maximum number of non-overlapping copies in the reduced representative of <math>g</math>. For example, <math>C_{aa}(aaaa)=3</math> and <math>c_{aa}(aaaa)=2</math>. Then, a '''big counting quasimorphism''' (resp. '''little counting quasimorphism''') is a function of the form <math>H_w(g)=C_w(g)-C_{w^{-1}}(g)</math> (resp. <math>h_w(g)=c_w(g)-c_{w^{-1}}(g))</math>.
* The [[rotation number]] <math>\widetilde{\text{rot}}:\widetilde{\text{Homeo}^+(S^1)}\to\mathbb{R}</math> is a quasimorphism, where <math>\text{Homeo}^+(S^1)</math> denotes the orientation-preserving [[homeomorphism]]s of the [[circle]], and <math>\widetilde{\text{Homeo}^+(S^1)}</math> denotes its universal covering.

== Homogeneous ==
A quasimorphism is '''homogeneous''' if <math>f(g^n)=nf(g)</math> for all <math>g\in G, n\in \mathbb{Z}</math>. It turns out the study of quasimorphisms can be reduced to the study of homogeneous quasimorphisms, as every quasimorphism <math>f:G\to\mathbb{R}</math> is a bounded distance away from a unique homogeneous quasimorphism <math>\overline{f}:G\to\mathbb{R}</math>, given by :
:<math>\overline{f}(g)=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f(g^n)}{n}</math>.
A homogeneous quasimorphism <math>f:G\to\mathbb{R}</math> has the following properties:
* It is constant on [[conjugacy class]]es, i.e. <math>f(g^{-1}hg)=f(h)</math> for all <math>g, h\in G</math>,
* If <math>G</math> is [[Abelian group|abelian]], then <math>f</math> is a group homomorphism. The above remark implies that in this case all quasimorphisms are "trivial".

== Integer-valued ==
One can also define quasimorphisms similarly in the case of a function <math>f:G\to\mathbb{Z}</math>. In this case, the above discussion about homogeneous quasimorphisms does not hold anymore, as the limit <math>\lim_{n\to\infty}f(g^n)/n</math> does not exist in <math>\mathbb{Z}</math> in general.

For example, for <math>\alpha\in\mathbb{R}</math>, the map <math>\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}:n\mapsto\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor</math> is a quasimorphism. There is a construction of the real numbers as a quotient of quasimorphisms <math>\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}</math> by an appropriate equivalence relation, see [[Construction of the real numbers#Construction from integers (Eudoxus reals)|Construction of the reals numbers from integers (Eudoxus reals)]].
